title: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORD IN HELL MAY BE “LORD”
paragraphs:
THE MOST TERRIFYING WORD IN HELL MAY BE “LORD”
Are There People in Hell Who Thought They Were Christians? Jesus Gave an Answer So Disturbing That Every Churchgoer Needs to Read It Before Assuming, “That Could Never Be Me.”
There is something more frightening than an atheist dying convinced there is no God.
It is a religious person dying convinced everything is right between them and God.
Someone who knew the songs.
Someone who said the prayers.
Someone who posted Bible verses.
Someone who called Jesus “Lord.”
Someone who knew how to raise a hand during worship, how to speak Christian language, how to look spiritual in front of other believers.
Someone who was absolutely certain that when the final moment came, Jesus would welcome them home.
And then they heard Him say otherwise.
That is not a horror story invented by a preacher trying to frighten people into religion.
Jesus Christ Himself warned about it.
Near the conclusion of the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said:
“Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι· Κύριε κύριε…”
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie kyrie…
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord…’”
Stop there.
Because those words destroy one of the most dangerous assumptions a religious person can make.
The people Jesus describes are not approaching Him saying, “We never believed in You.”
They call Him Κύριε — Kyrie — Lord.
Twice.
“Lord, Lord.”
They sound certain.
They sound religious.
They apparently expect acceptance.
Yet Jesus continues that not everyone who calls Him Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of His Father in heaven.
Then the scene becomes even more unsettling.
Jesus says many will speak to Him on “that day.”
Not a tiny handful.
Many.
And they will appeal to extraordinary religious accomplishments performed in His name: prophecy, casting out demons, mighty works.
Imagine the confidence behind that defense.
Jesus, look at everything we did.
Look at our ministry.
Look at our spiritual experiences.
Look at the things associated with Your name.
And then comes one of the most devastating sentences recorded in Scripture:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “I knew you once, but then I forgot you.”
He says:
Οὐδέποτε — never.
“I never knew you.”
And suddenly the question is no longer merely, “Are there people in hell who thought they were Christians?”
The question becomes painfully personal:
Could someone know Christian language without truly knowing Christ?
According to Jesus, yes.
That should not make sincere believers spend every waking moment terrified that one imperfect day has erased the grace of God.
But it should destroy casual presumption.
Because there is a counterfeit Christianity that can exist remarkably close to the real thing.
You can know about Jesus without belonging to Jesus.
You can admire Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
You can defend Christian morality while secretly loving the sin Christ calls you to forsake.
You can inherit Christianity culturally without ever being born again spiritually.
You can have Christian parents.
Christian friends.
A Christian playlist.
A baptism certificate.
A favorite preacher.
A shelf full of Bibles.
And still miss Christ Himself.
That is the scandal.
But please keep reading, because the answer is not where many people expect it to be.
The answer is not “Try harder until Jesus loves you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
Scripture does not teach that sinners purchase salvation with religious performance.
Paul writes that we are saved by grace through faith, and that this is not our own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so nobody can boast.
The thief beside Jesus could not build a ministry résumé.
He could not spend twenty years proving himself.
He could not undo his past.
He could not climb down from his cross and repair everything he had destroyed.
He had nothing impressive left to offer.
Only a guilty man…
and a crucified King.
And Jesus gave him hope.
That is grace.
The Gospel is not God standing at the top of a mountain shouting, “Climb high enough and perhaps I will accept you.”
The Gospel is the Son of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
Jesus lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And sinners are summoned to repent and believe the Gospel.
That means the frightening people of Matthew 7 are not rejected because they failed to accumulate enough impressive religious achievements.
Read their defense again.
Their achievements are exactly what they appeal to.
“Did we not…?”
“Did we not…?”
“Did we not…?”
Their confidence is wrapped around what they did.
Jesus brings the issue back to relationship with Him:
“I never knew you.”
That distinction matters enormously.
Biblical obedience is not the purchase price of salvation.
It is fruit that belongs to a living faith.
We are not saved because we became impressive enough.
We are saved by the grace of God through faith in Christ, and the Christ who saves us does not leave us contentedly married to the sin from which He came to redeem us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Repentance does not mean becoming sinlessly perfect overnight.
It means there has been a fundamental change of direction toward God. When the Christian falls, he does not rename darkness “light” merely so he can remain comfortable inside it.
He comes back to Christ.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes ashamed.
Sometimes after a terrible failure.
Sometimes whispering the only prayer he can manage:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is a massive difference between struggling against sin and making peace with sin.
A believer may stumble.
Peter did.
A believer may experience terrible weakness.
The disciples did.
A believer may need correction, restoration, discipline, forgiveness, and repeated reminders of grace.
The New Testament assumes Christians still need all of those things.
But the dangerous heart says:
I want Jesus as Savior, but nobody will tell me He is Lord.
I want forgiveness, but I refuse repentance.
I want heaven, but I do not want Christ interfering with the throne of my life.
That is why this subject cannot be reduced to, “Did you once repeat a prayer?”
The issue is not whether your mouth once produced Christian words.
The issue is where your hope rests.
Paul told the Corinthians:
“Ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἑαυτοὺς δοκιμάζετε…”
Heautous peirazete ei este en tē pistei, heautous dokimazete…
“Examine yourselves… test yourselves.”
Biblical self-examination is not an invitation to become obsessed with yourself until you despair.
It should drive you toward truth.
Where is your confidence before God?
Your morality?
Your baptism?
Your denomination?
Your ministry?
Your generosity?
Your theology?
Your church attendance?
Your Facebook posts?
Your good intentions?
Or Jesus Christ?
Because when death strips everything else away, Christ is not merely something Christians possess.
Christ is all we have.
And perhaps somebody reading this has just become uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because fear itself can save you.
It cannot.
But because false assurance is too dangerous to protect merely because exposing it hurts.
Suppose a physician discovers something deadly but treatable inside you.
Would love remain silent because the diagnosis might ruin your afternoon?
No.
Love tells the truth because your life matters.
Jesus warns because eternity matters.
And His warnings are surrounded by invitations of grace.
The same Jesus who speaks of judgment also says that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
Think about that.
The answer to discovering that your Christianity has been hollow is not to run away from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Maybe you have been pretending.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe pornography owns a secret room in your life and you have protected it for years.
Bring it into the light and come to Jesus.
Maybe everybody thinks your marriage is beautiful while cruelty lives behind the closed door.
Repent and come to Jesus.
Maybe you preach grace publicly while feeding pride privately.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize it as poison.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years trying to look saved rather than asking whether you have truly trusted the Savior.
Come to Jesus.
You do not need a cleaner past before you approach Him.
You need Christ.
This is what makes the Gospel so breathtaking.
Christianity begins with a scandal.
God does not save the deserving.
There are no deserving people to save.
“All have sinned.”
The cross humiliates human pride because it announces that our condition was so desperate that the Son of God had to die…
and then it overwhelms human despair because it announces that the Son of God was willing to die.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses have admitted.
His grace is greater than your shame has imagined.
That is the movement from scandal to grace.
Look at Peter.
He boasted that he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
A servant girl.
A question.
Fear.
Denial.
Again.
Again.
And somewhere in the darkness, a rooster crowed.
Imagine the sound.
Peter had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had confessed Jesus as the Christ.
And then, when loyalty became expensive, Peter denied even knowing Him.
What do you do with a disciple like that?
If Christianity were merely a religion of human performance, Peter's story should have ended beside that charcoal fire.
Failure.
Disqualified.
Finished.
But Jesus was not finished.
After the resurrection, Christ restored the man who had denied Him.
Peter's sin mattered.
Peter's repentance mattered.
But Peter's failure did not prove stronger than Christ's restoring grace.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Not permission to continue hiding.
Permission to finally stop hiding.
You have performed long enough.
You have smiled long enough.
You have told everybody, “I'm okay,” long enough.
Jesus already knows.
The addiction.
The affair.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The private fantasies.
The arrogance.
The hypocrisy.
The prayerlessness.
The unbelief you are afraid to admit.
The wound that made you angry at God.
The church hurt you never processed.
The shame you buried underneath religious activity.
He knows.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come.
Not tomorrow when you feel more spiritual.
Now.
There is another side of this warning that must be said carefully.
Do not read Matthew 7 and conclude that every trembling Christian is secretly damned.
The people Jesus describes display remarkable confidence in their religious credentials.
Meanwhile, some genuine believers are painfully aware of their weakness.
Your grief over sin does not save you, but neither is spiritual struggle automatically evidence that Christ has abandoned you.
The Christian's assurance rests ultimately in Christ and His promises, while Scripture also teaches that genuine faith bears fruit.
Not flawless fruit.
Real fruit.
A changed relationship with sin.
Love for Christ.
Growing obedience.
Perseverance.
Love for other believers.
Confession when we fall.
A heart that keeps being drawn back to the Savior.
Not perfection.
Direction.
Not earning.
Evidence.
Not “Look how worthy I have become.”
But:
“Look how merciful Jesus has been to me.”
And this is where the question in the title becomes unavoidable.
Are there people in hell who thought they were Christians?
Jesus' warning in Matthew 7 gives us sobering reason to answer:
Yes.
People can possess a false assurance.
People can call Him “Lord” while never truly belonging to Him.
People can point to religious activity and still hear, “I never knew you.”
Jesus also speaks plainly about final judgment. In Matthew 25:41 the Greek text speaks of “τὸ πῦρ τὸ αἰώνιον” — to pyr to aiōnion — “the eternal fire,” prepared for the devil and his angels.
Hell is not something Christians should discuss with smugness.
If we believe Jesus, we should speak about judgment with tears in our eyes and the Gospel on our lips.
Because nobody reading this article is beyond the reach of Christ merely because their past is scandalous.
The cross was built for guilty people.
That means this article is not asking you merely:
“Are you scared of hell?”
A person can fear punishment without loving Christ.
The deeper question is:
Do you want Jesus?
Not merely His benefits.
Not merely heaven.
Not merely protection from judgment.
Jesus.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The Shepherd.
The King.
The Lord.
The Savior.
Do you trust Him?
Because someday the filters disappear.
The titles disappear.
The follower count disappears.
The bank account disappears.
The reputation disappears.
The applause disappears.
Even the carefully constructed version of ourselves that other people believed disappears.
And there we stand before God.
Nothing left to curate.
Nothing left to perform.
Nothing left to hide behind.
So do not wait until eternity to become honest about what is happening in your soul today.
Not as a magic formula.
Not because typing words into Facebook saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needed to see.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, do not weaponize this article against them.
Do not send it with the attitude, See? This is about you.
Open the Bible.
Read the Sermon on the Mount in context.
Test everything written here against Scripture.
Truth does not need us to be afraid of examination.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, heal from failure, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close.
God cannot be purchased, salvation cannot be bought, and nobody earns spiritual favor by supporting a ministry.
But believers can glorify God by faithfully using the resources He has entrusted to them to help sound Gospel work reach people.
But never confuse supporting Gospel ministry with the Gospel itself.
You can buy every Christian book ever printed and still need Jesus.
You can wear a Christian shirt, drink from a Bible-verse mug, fill journals with prayers, attend conferences, quote theology, defend Christianity online…
and still the center remains exactly where Scripture places it:
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling people to repent and believe.
Offering forgiveness that cannot be purchased.
Giving grace that cannot be earned.
Transforming people who could never rewrite themselves.
So tonight, before you ask whether somebody else is a “real Christian,” bring the question home.
Ask Christ to search you.
Ask Him to expose counterfeit confidence.
Ask Him to uncover cherished sin.
Ask Him to break religious pride.
Ask Him to teach you genuine repentance.
Ask Him to make the Gospel precious again.
And when He exposes something ugly, do not run into hiding like Adam.
Run toward the Savior whose hands still bear the scars of redemption.
Because perhaps the most terrifying possibility is reaching the end having spent a lifetime knowing Christian things without knowing Christ.
But perhaps the most beautiful possibility is realizing, while there is still breath in your lungs, that you have been pretending…
and finally coming home.
There is grace for the hypocrite who repents.
Grace for the addict who comes into the light.
Grace for the proud.
Grace for the sexually broken.
Grace for the bitter.
Grace for the churchgoer.
Grace for the skeptic.
Grace for the prodigal.
Grace for the person whose Christianity has been little more than a costume.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that restores.
Grace that changes people.
Grace with nail-scarred hands.
So be honest.
Did this hit harder than you expected?
Because somewhere tonight, somebody thinks they have gone too far.
Somebody thinks their hypocrisy has permanently disqualified them.
Somebody is terrified that if Jesus knew the entire story, He would want nothing to do with them.
But Jesus already knows the entire story.
The question is whether we will keep hiding from Him…
or finally fall at His feet.
The most frightening words would be “I never knew you”—but while Christ is calling you today, your story does not have to end with those words.
